chunks: How I2C transactions work step by step. The question: How does it work? Explain its operation.
An I2C transaction is a fixed script on the two wires. The controller signals START, sends the address of the chip it wants plus a read-or-write bit, and waits for an acknowledge.
Then bytes flow, each followed by an acknowledge bit, and the controller signals STOP. Both wires sit high when idle. Data may change only while the clock is low.
START and STOP are the only exceptions.
Picture a drive-through window. You pull up, which is START. You name the window you want (the address) and hear "OK" (the acknowledge).
You say your order, one item at a time, and each gets an "OK". On your last item you say "that's all", which is a NACK. Then you drive off, which is STOP.
On a real bus, "OK" is the receiver pulling the data wire low for one clock tick.
A read-direction frame.

The address byte (0x48, 1001000) with R = 1 is driven by the controller; on the ninth clock the target ACKs; then the target drives the first data byte (0x0C here) and the controller's ACK would follow.
Look for the rule: every SDA transition sits in an SCL-low window.
START and STOP: special moves of the data wire while the clock is high. START begins a transaction and STOP ends it.
Address byte: the 7-bit address of the chip, plus one bit saying read or write ("I2C address and data frames").
Read/write bit: 0 means the controller will write, and 1 means it will read. ACK and NACK: the receiver's reply on the ninth clock.
ACK is the data wire pulled low, and NACK is left high ("I2C ACK and NACK"). Repeated START: a new START without a STOP before it, which keeps the bus claimed.

To read two bytes from register 0 of the chip at address 0x48, the controller sends START, 0x90 (hexadecimal for the address with the write bit), register number 0x00, a repeated START, and 0x91 (the address with the read bit).
Then it clocks in two bytes. That is 5 bytes at 9 clock ticks each, 45 ticks, about 112 microseconds at 400 kilohertz.
The controller ACKs the first byte, NACKs the last, then sends STOP. That is the whole idea.
"Both lines idle high.
The controller pulls SDA low while SCL is high, that's START, then clocks out a 7-bit address and a read/write bit, MSB first, changing SDA only while SCL is low.
On the ninth clock the addressed device pulls SDA low to ACK. Data bytes follow, each with its own ACK; on a read the controller NACKs the last byte.
A STOP, SDA rising while SCL is high, ends it. Register reads use a repeated START between the pointer write and the read."
